item.description:
August 2023 • Columbus City Council

2023 Council Housing Initiatives Update

Housing is a Human Right. Earlier this year, in March, City Council announced our 2023 Housing Initiatives, a package of 12 policy proposals with the intent to increase renter protections and homeownership opportunities. This collaborative effort builds upon the work started with the 2021 Housing for All legislative package I sponsored through my role as Chair of Council’s Housing Committee.

 

As we know all too well, Columbus is facing a housing crisis. Between 2016 and 2022, the average rent for a two-bedroom unit skyrocketed from $831 to $1,295, a 56% increase. This is not sustainable. Already, our housing market has left far too many families behind, pricing them out of safe, quality, and stable housing. I am committed to the idea that housing is a human right and have spent my time on Council trying to put that principle into practice.

 

In just four months since the rollout of this 12-piece plan, we have already passed half or 6 of the 12 initiatives. These include:

 

  1. Retaliatory Action Protections: This legislation aims to encourage renters to call 311 for any violations in their rental property with the goal to prevent predatory practices.
  2. Pay to Stay Legislation: This legislation would allow residents time to secure rental assistance dollars up until a court judgment.
  3. 3rd Party Payment Legislation: Legislation would require landlords to accept a third-party payment on behalf of a tenant if that tenant is not in breach of their rental agreement.
  4. $1M in Homeownership Opportunities Funding: This initiative will provide funding support to low-income families and individuals, making homeownership more attainable.
  5. $1.5M in funding for Eviction Court Legal Representation Guarantee: Tenants with legal representation are much more likely to avoid an eviction judgment. In 2022, Council legislated $1.5M to create a more robust legal representation team at eviction court. This additional $1.5M will allow this work to continue.
  6. Owner/Occupied Initiative Program: This program will expand home repair grants to homeowners to include roof repairs. Home repairs, especially roof repairs pose significant hurdles for seniors to be able to age in place. This legislation prioritizes housing preservation through repair, not demolition.

 

Over the next few months, Council will work on passing the last 6 of the initiatives. However, the passage of these initiatives does not mark the end of my advocacy on the issue of affordable housing. The Housing for All package and the 2023 Council Housing Initiatives are just the beginning. A complex problem requires a comprehensive solution, and these 15 initiatives are not a silver bullet; we have to constantly search and advocate for innovative and progressive solutions that address the looming housing crisis.

 

For more information, check out the Council’s website: 2023 Housing Initiatives (columbus.gov)

 

Housing for All: 2nd Annual Housing Forum

In 2021, I sponsored the Housing for All legislative package with the intent to increase the breadth and depth of renter protections within the City. This package included three critical pieces of legislation:

  1. Rental Receipts Requirements: Requires building owners to provide renters with a receipt of any rental payments.
  2. Renter’s Choice: Enabling renters to pay off a security deposit in increments rather than all-at-once.
  3. Source of Income Protections: Prohibits building owners from discriminating against prospective renters on the basis of the source of their income.

 

Passing renter protections is important, but equally important is ensuring residents understand their rights granted with these new regulations. Thus, we launched the Housing for All Campaign, an education and marketing effort to ensure that landlords understand the laws they must follow and that renters understand the protections they are guaranteed. This year, we continued our second year of the campaign with the intent to continue our community outreach efforts and solicit feedback on what we as public servants can do to continue making our housing space more inclusive of all residents.

 

On July 12th, we held our 2nd annual Housing for All Forum, a town-hall that brought together stakeholders from across the housing spectrum to discuss potential solutions to Columbus’s housing crisis. With over 200 attendees, this event was a massive success, and we even had an out-of-state keynote: Sonja Trauss, Executive Director of YIMBY Law.

 

If we want to live in a progressive community that truly uplifts ALL of our neighbors, we have to take action. Housing is a human right; we must work as a community to ensure all people have access to it. If you want to keep updated on the Housing for All campaign, check out our website: Housing for All Columbus | housing resources | Columbus, OH, USA (housingforallcbus.com)

 

Did you know...

Since 2020, over 56,000 evictions have been filed in Franklin County alone. Rentful614 is a rental assistance resource for tenants and landlords to ensure housing stability for those struggling to pay their utilities or rent bills! Check it out: https://www.rentful614.com/

 

Community Outreach

Over the course of 8 months, I have sponsored 20 resolutions to recognize a number of occasions and organizations throughout the City of Columbus. We are a diverse community, and it is one of the great pleasures of my job to have the opportunity to shine a spotlight on exemplary organizations or increase awareness of particular causes. If you want to request a resolution from my office, please feel free to reach out to tjlittlejohn@columbus.gov!

 

I have also had the opportunity to attend a number of events throughout the community, including those hosted by the South Side Thrive Collaborative, the American Institute of Architects, and Stonewall Columbus. As a public servant, I view it as my responsibility to be accessible to you, my constituents. My job is to empower and uplift you, and community engagement events are just one touchpoint in which I can understand what I should advocate for on Council. If you want to request a meeting or for my presence at an event, please reach out to knasiedu@columbus.gov!

 

In the pipeline…

Throughout the rest of the year, City Council still has a host of initiatives that we are excited to implement. At the top of that list: passing the last 6 of Council’s Housing Initiatives. These include:

  1. Rent Increase Notification: Increasing the amount of time between when a landlord notifies their tenant of a rent increase and when that increase can take effect.
  1. Vacant and Foreclosure Registry: A registry would give the ability to have up-to-date contact information for the owners of foreclosed or vacant properties and legally hold property owners responsible for leaving abandoned properties in disrepair
  2. Housing Wholesaler Regulations: This legislation would create licensed regulations similar to that of a realtor to prevent predatory practices.
  3. Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) Pilot Program: This program will focus on the creation of affordable accessory dwelling units on lots that currently house one single-unit dwelling. Adding an ADU doubles the amount of housing units at a low cost to the primary landowner.
  4. Rental Registry: A Rental Registration Program will protect the wellbeing of our residents and encourage both owners and occupants to maintain and improve the quality of rental housing. With the collection of a rental registration fee, millions of dollars will be generated and used for rental assistance, thus providing an “insurance policy” for landlords.
  5. Office of Fair Housing: legislation that would create a robust fair housing office to hold landlords/property owners accountable and to protect the rights of tenants.

 

We are also excited to be welcoming the 2023-2024 Columbus Youth Council Cohort! This program has been near to my heart since its first iteration in 2019. Seeing so many young people learn and grow in their advocacy skills and understanding of local government is truly inspiring, and I know this incoming cohort will prove to be just as exceptional as the previous.

 

In the rest of this newsletter, you will read more about happenings in the City Council and in my Office. As always, I represent you and would love to hear your thoughts! Please feel free to reach out to my office at 614-645-5524.

Black Business Highlight

Dr. Melissa Crum is an award-winning certified diversity and inclusion practitioner and executive coach who helps mission-driven organizations experience radical and sustainable growth by shifting belief patterns. She is an artist, author, researcher, and founder of the consulting company, Mosaic Education Network. Mosaic infuses the arts, research, storytelling, and critical thinking into professional development, community building, and curriculum development.

 

Dr. Crum has facilitated training sessions across the U.S., creating a non-judgmental and refreshingly honest look at privileges and privately held beliefs. Her workshops focus on workplace culture development, equipping educators, leadership, staff, and board members with the skills to implement inclusive and equitable practices.

 

By creating a brave space, Dr. Crum’s workshops allow organizations to critically investigate policies, workplace and learning culture, and relationship dynamics. Together, she empowers teams to positively dismantle systemic patterns, build authentic communication, and instigate radical growth company-wide. To learn more, visit www.mosaiceducationnetwork.com

Council Spotlight

  1. On July 31st, Council passed Pay to Stay legislation, a policy that will provide tenants a defense to an eviction for nonpayment of rent, if the tenant tenders to the landlord, and the landlord refuses to accept, (1) all past due rent, and (2) reasonable late fees. The tender can be after the eviction is filed but before the court issues a judgment.
    1. Ohio is just one of five states where property owners can give tenants a three-day notice to leave or face eviction proceedings, and landlords are not required to accept rent payment during this time.
    2. This is a key protection for renters to increase their housing stability. Pay to Stay is 1 of the 12 policies part of Council’s 2023 Housing Initiatives, one I am proud to have sponsored.
  2. At our July 31st meeting, Council also approved Third Party Payment legislation, an initiative that would require landlords accept payment on behalf of a tenant so long as they are not in breach of their rental agreement. Failure to accept payment will be deemed as an affirmative defense in any eviction action filed against the tenant for non-payment of rent.

Committee Highlight

Health & Human Services

  1. On July 17th, Council approved a total of $4,550,000 in grant money to 44 social service agencies located in Columbus as part of the Elevate 1.0 grant program, an initiative with the goal to support and increase the organizational capacity of non-profit organizations that experienced revenue losses caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. 2022 was the first year of the three years Elevate 1.0 program with the grants awarded under this legislation being known as Elevate 1.0, Year 2.
    • Forty-eight community agencies were recommended for the $5,000,000.00 (5 million) in available funding, with forty-four included in this ordinance.
    • This legislation invests $5 million dollars of City of Columbus ARPA funds to increase the organizational capacity of nonprofit organizations tackling homelessness, infant mortality rates, and increasing housing stability for immigrant and refugee households.

Housing

  1. On July 31st, Council approved $1M in funding for the purpose of providing homeownership opportunities for lower-income households. The ultimate goal of this three-fold: provide financial support for households to be able to own their own home, create generational wealth for communities that have been disenfranchised, and increase housing stability among lower-income and minority residents.
    • This initiative was a part of Council’s 2023 Housing Initiatives and was led by Councilmember Barroso de Padilla.
  2. City Council also voted in favor of the Owner/Occupied Initiative Program (OOIP), another policy part of the 2023 Housing Initiatives. The OOIP, when implemented, would allow senior citizens to remain in their homes and maintain their generational wealth by providing funding for home repairs. The ultimate goal of this program is to prioritize housing preservation through repair, not demolition.
    • This legislation is a key part of upholding the preservation tenant of this year’s Council Housing Initiatives, with the policy led by Councilmember Brown’s office.  
  3. As part of the City’s operational budget, Council approved $1.5M in funding to ensure that all tenants are provided with legal representation at Eviction Court. On July 31st, City Council voted to appropriate this money to Columbus Legal Aid. 
    • It is estimated that 90% of landlords are represented by legal counsel in evictions, but fewer than 10% of tenants have legal representation. This disparity creates an unequal playing field in court as those with legal representation are much more likely to avoid an eviction judgment.

Criminal Justice & Judiciary

  1. On July 10th, Council voted to authorize the Franklin County Municipal Court to accept a grant in the amount of $2,589,856 from the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction. The grant money will be used to aid the Court’s efforts to reduce the number of offenders on probation supervision who violate the condition of their supervision through funding the salaries and benefits of 15 existing probation officers.
    • These officers will provide pretrial assessments and supervision to defendants in custody awaiting arraignment in the Municipal Court and perform specialized supervision of individuals placed on electronic monitoring.  
    • The program will only include defendants appearing in Municipal Court arraignment in custody for criminal misdemeanor and/or operating a vehicle while impaired (OVI).

July 2023 • Columbus City Council

Happy Disability Pride Month!

On July 26th, 1990, the Americans with Disabilities act was signed into law, ensuring that those with disabilities are not hindered in their journey for success and self-fulfillment. Every July, we honor the ratification of this legislation and take the time to recognize the achievements and historical contributions of Americans with disabilities. But, most importantly, we continue to fight towards the ideal that each of us, regardless of ability, are worthy of equal dignity, respect, and opportunity.

 

AmeriDisability describes disability pride as, “accepting and honoring each person's uniqueness and seeing it as a natural and beautiful part of human diversity." It is a concept connected with the idea of disability justice, a movement toward eliminating the barriers of oppression that those living with disabilities face on a daily basis. This includes ensuring we provide the necessary tools, like healthcare and workforce development, for those who need it. It also means we must be intentional in hearing out the community for their needs, something the City of Columbus does in part through the Columbus Advisory Committee on Disability Issues (CACDI).

 

Our efforts to uplift the voices of those living with a disability should not occur only during a single month, but rather we should be making a concerted effort to empower them to have their voices heard. The community is diverse, and their respective needs are unique. We as a city must acknowledge this fact and pursue policy initiatives that ensure the needs of each of our residents is met.

 

In the rest of this newsletter, you will read more about happenings in the City Council and in my Office. As always, I represent you and would love to hear your thoughts! Please feel free to reach out to my office at 614-645-5524.

Mark Your Calendar: Housing for All Forum (July 12th)

Check out the new look for the Housing For All initiative. The new website (housingforallcbus.com) will be a hub for Columbus residents to visit for updates regarding City Council Housing Initiatives, Housing For All Events, and resources related to housing support. Please visit and subscribe so that you receive all the updates!

 

The next event coming up will be our 2nd Annual Housing Forum and you’re invited! Here are some of the details:

  • When: July 12, 2023 | 5:00pm – 8:00pm
  • Where: Columbus State Community College – Mitchell Hall (250 Cleveland Ave Columbus, OH 43205) 
    • Accessible by COTA Line 10

The Housing For All Annual Housing Forum aims to bring together experts, policymakers, advocates, and stakeholders within the housing sector to discuss our most pressing issues and explore innovative solutions towards achieving the goal of affordable and sustainable housing for all across our growing city. This forum will serve as a platform for understanding the latest housing policies and programs under Housing For All and how our city is taking action to protect both tenants and housing providers, along with access to resources for forum attendees.

 

Our keynote speaker is Sonya Trauss, Executive Director of YIMBY Law, which is a project of Yes In My Back Yard. Make sure you follow us on social media as we share more about all our amazing speakers! 

 

Please RSVP here to make sure you’re there!

Black Women Equal Pay Day (July 27th)

It is estimated that Black Women earn just $0.67 to a White Man’s $1.00. This figure is emblematic of a larger, more systemic issue perpetuating economic inequality: women and people of color are often paid less than their male and/or white colleagues for doing the same job. This issue is further compounded by the fact that Black Women find themselves overrepresented in lower-paying occupations, a fact exacerbated by the COVID-19 Pandemic. I, along with the rest of the City of Columbus, is committed to eliminating this gap and ensuring that all people can lead a self-fulfilling and economically stable life. As such, I am excited to promote the Black Women’s Equal Pay Day Signing Event hosted by the Columbus Women’s Commission at Adelphi Bank, Ohio’s first Black-owned bank.

 

For more information, please check out this link: Black Women's Equal Pay Day Tickets, Thu, Jul 27, 2023 at 4:30 PM | Eventbrite

Disability Advocacy Highlight

Open Door Columbus

For more than four decades, Open Door has been dedicated to our mission of inspiring life journeys for adults with disabilities in central Ohio. We cultivate valued roles for all people through a variety of residential services, community-based adult day programs, employment services, and accessible transportation options.

Our mindset is focused on affirming the needs and goals of the individuals we support. We know that every person is valuable, with a unique story, desires, and ambitions. We see ourselves as a vehicle to help them on life’s journey, wherever that may lead.

 

This is particularly true for the folks we support who are part of the LGBTQ+ community. Marcie, an individual in our Supported Community Living program, is a member of the trans community and has faced significant difficulties getting the care and basic respect she deserves. Other providers she worked with did not understand that she identified as female and were unwilling to help with her goal of changing her name.

 

Then Marcie came to Open Door. Our staff diligently helped her fill out applications, find proper documentation, and make court visits. And recently, her name change became official.

 

“I finally felt like a whole person,” she said. “I had a lot of help from my staff. They were always there for me.”

 

We were proud to help Marcie express her identity. As we celebrate Disability Pride Month, Open Door recognizes the immense value of the diversity of the individuals we support. We’ll continue to inspire and affirm others while advocating to make our community a safer, more accessible place for all.

 

Council Spotlight

  • On June 5th, Council approved $442,775 in funding to 4 nonprofits organizations with the purpose of expanding youth Summer programming within the City.
    • The four organizations that received the funding are: Africentric Personal Development Shop, Inc. ($38,775.00), Community Arts Project Inc. DBA The Kings Arts Complex ($100,000.00), The Columbus Urban League ($300,000.00), Youth Development of Columbus ($4,000.00)
  • At our June 5th meeting, City Council approved $70,000 in funding to the Columbus Division of Police for their Teens and Police Service Partners (TAPS) program.
    • The TAPS program serves at-risk youth between ages 13-17 at four middle and high schools. The program provides those participating with a structured environment that is geared to mentor through an academic and humanitarian approach, with strong emphasis on interaction and conversation. 
  • On June 26th, Council accepted a $2M grant from the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation to fund the “Reimagining Columbus” project.The “Reimagining Columbus” project seeks to:
    • Host conversations to understand what Columbus residents value most, and how the city’s future symbology and public art landscape can communicate shared values and aspirations.
    • Provide the public with opportunities to collaboratively ideate on the future disposition of the Christopher Columbus statue, and with requisite community buy-in, design a new space that allows the public to understand and physically interact with difficult history.

Committee Highlights

Health & Human Services

  • City Council approved $45K in funding to Columbus Public Health for the purchase of gun lock boxes, each of which will be distributed at no cost to residents of the city.
    • Last year, City Council passed 3 pieces of common sense gun legislation, one of these was Safe Storage. This legislation penalized those who fail to exercise due care in storing their firearms. 
    • In 2022, Columbus Public Health gave away more than 1,000 safe storage lock boxes. To help strengthen this work we are investing $45,000 to purchase additional gun lock boxes for any resident who is in need of one.

Housing

  • On June 12th, Council voted to name The Wells Foundation as the Fiscal Manager for the $26M in Emergency Rental Assistance 2 (ERA 2) dollars the City of Columbus received from the Federal Government. 
    • These dollars will be used to assist renters struggling to make rent or utility payments and ensure they can remain in stable housing conditions.
    • The ERA 2 grant is in addition to $60M+ ERA 1 and ERA 2 funds the City has already disbursed through 36 nonprofit partners.

Criminal Justice & Judiciary

  • At the June 12th meeting, City Council approved a settlement in the amount of $32,414.03 in the case, City of Long Beach, et al. v. Monsanto Company, et al.
    • Columbus joined 12 other cities and municipalities against the Monsanto Company for their usage of polychlorinated biphenyls (“PCBs”), a known environmental toxin.

June 2023 • Councilmember Shayla Favor

Gun Violence Awareness

Since 2010, gun violence has taken the lives of more than 1,300 Columbus residents. Gun violence is an epidemic in this city, one that touches the lives of each of us, a fact we know all too well given the events of the past month. All people deserve the right to feel safe in their homes, schools, and neighborhoods, yet the proliferation of gun violence threatens such rights, and has created a culture of fear that degrades individuals’ mental well-being, especially our youths’. 

 

While recent coverage of gun violence within Columbus has focused on the Short North, this is an issue that affects each neighborhood within the city. The same night 10 were injured in the Short North, an individual from the South Side and South Linden, respectively, were fatally injured due to guns. If we are to address this issue, we must do so as a city, ensuring that any effort is not focused on just one neighborhood, but instead combating gun violence across the entire community.

 

Despite opposition from the Statehouse, City Council has taken strides against gun violence, passing legislation last December to prohibit the sale of high-capacity rifles within Columbus and codifying certain firearm storage standards. Further, we have provided Columbus Public Health with funding to distribute gun lock boxes to residents free-of-charge. Though these are important steps, they are certainly just a starting point. To tackle this epidemic, we must take a more active role in preventing such instances of violence from occurring. This is a two-pronged approach: reducing the number of guns within Columbus, and ensuring all people have a basic standard of living so that they do not feel the need to resort to such violence.

 

Given the circumstances, we will not be able to solve this problem overnight, but rest assured, my colleagues and myself have and will continue to work tirelessly to ensure the safety of all of our residents. I hope you join us in this fight.

 

In the rest of this newsletter, you will read more about happenings in the City Council and in my Office. As always, I represent you and would love to hear your thoughts! Please feel free to reach out to my office at 614-645-5524.

Let's 'band together to fight for our reproductive freedom'

 

Abortion care IS healthcare. Full stop. 

 

On May 10th, the Columbus dispatch ran a letter to the editor written by Councilmember Barroso de Padilla and me in which we outline our unwavering support for Ohioans For Reproductive Freedom’s campaign to preserve reproductive rights through the Ohio Constitution.

 

Last year, we announced our 4-piece legislative package to secure reproductive care for all Columbus residents. Now, we’re joining the cause to ensure access for all Ohioans.

 

I urge you to visit ohioansforreproductivefreedom.org to learn how you can join the fight!

LGBTQ+ Advocacy Highlight

Kaleidoscope Youth Center

Kaleidoscope Youth Center (KYC)  is Ohio's largest and longest-serving organization solely dedicated to supporting LGBTQIA+ youth ages 12 - 24. Services include a drop-in center, community education and training, advocacy and civic engagement, health and wellness programs, and housing opportunities. As a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, KYC works to provide safer spaces so youth can be free to explore who they are and empowered to become their confident, truest self.

 

Our commitment to creating safer spaces extends beyond the walls of 603 East Town Street in Columbus. We believe in the humanity and dignity of every young person, and we are committed to fighting anti-LGBTQIA+ legislation and policies. Our advocacy uplifts the voices of LGBTQIA+ youth, who are directly impacted by these bills but often aren’t able to testify.

 

In the last year, KYC staff testified at the State Board of Education against its anti-LGBTQIA+ resolution, and at the Ohio Statehouse against bills that would prevent transgender youth from playing school sports and accessing gender-affirming care, and a bill requiring schools to “out” students to their families and share other personal information – even if doing so poses a risk to students’ safety. We have regular discussions with KYC youth about these issues and use their opinions to help inform our stances as an organization. We also host advocacy meetings to help youth become more civically engaged. Find a list of bills that we’re watching and learn how to take action at www.kycohio.org/advocacy. 

 

We use our social media to educate others about how to stay engaged with the legislative process. Our podcast, Speaking Queerly, also amplifies the voices and stories of LGBTQIA+ youth, advocates and allies. You can follow KYC on all social media platforms (@KYCOhio), and listen to our podcast on Spotify and Apple Podcasts

2023 Columbus Youth Council Applications are Live!

In 2019, I had the honor to spearhead the Columbus Youth Council (CYC), a program to provide Columbus High School juniors and seniors with an opportunity to immerse themselves in city government and learn how they can become stewards in their community. If selected, students will participate in educational opportunities to learn more about the structure of city government, public policy, public safety, and much more. The program doubles as a professional development opportunity too, with students being afforded the opportunity to interact with various community leaders, including members of the Columbus City Council.

And, with the 2022-2023 academic year coming to an end, I am excited to announce that the application to be a part of our 2023-2024 cohort is now live! For more information on the program, please visit: www.columbus.gov/cyc/

    • These funds will go to two organizations, The Columbus Urban League and Community for New Direction, with each receiving about $430K to help fund their intervention navigators, individuals that meet with victims and their families after a violent incident.

    • This fund provides financial assistance to enable expanded access for family planning services including contraceptives, cancer screenings, and sexual health.
    • This appropriation was necessary to enable Columbus Public Health to accept a $700K grant from the Ohio Department of Health, with program fees estimated to generate $950K in revenue.

Housing

  • On May 15th, Council passed an ordinance enabling the City’s Land Bank program to acquire a parcel on Mound Street to consolidate into a larger tract of land for an affordable housing project.
    • This acquisition will aid affordable housing partners to qualify Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC), expand existing Land Trusts, and construct other affordable housing.
    • This legislation will authorize the Director of the Department of Development to execute any and all documents that are necessary to acquire property, as approved by the City Attorney’s Office, and spend an amount not to exceed $20,000.00.

Criminal Justice & Judiciary

This grant will be used to partially fund the salaries of two victim assistance staff for the continuation of a program to assist probation officers in domestic violence units.

    • This ordinance would authorize the transfer to and expenditure of $500,000.000 from the Health Operating Fund to support ROOTT’s Preinatal Support Doula care.

April 04, 2023 • Columbus City Council

Happy Fair Housing Month!

Affordable, quality housing is a right, not a privilege. Full-stop. In April, we celebrate National Fair Housing Month-a time to recommit ourselves to the goal of achieving equity in housing and homeownership opportunities. Fair Housing Month was established to commemorate the passage of the Fair Housing Act which prohibited discrimination in housing transactions. With our population predicted to grow two-fold and our housing stock remaining stagnant, the City of Columbus is facing a housing crisis. We are not building enough affordable housing to meet demand, and our most marginalized communities stand to be disproportionately affected. As such, I am proud to be sponsoring a resolution to name April National Fair Housing Month, in Columbus as a commitment to promoting equal opportunity in housing.

 

Lack of affordable housing is linked to a number of public problems including, increased unsheltered populations, worsening of health outcomes, lower household wealth, and heightened food insecurity. In fact, the Joint Center for Housing Studies found that nearly one in three households spend more than 30% of their monthly income on housing-related expenses, with renters spending upwards of 50%. As households spend more money on paying for housing, they are left with less and less to spend on other necessities like food and healthcare. Our current housing landscape is an unequal playing field: those with less means are systematically disadvantaged, and, as time goes on, the gap enlarges. 

 

The City of Columbus has a history of discriminating against BIPOC within the housing market: redlining them out of homeownership opportunities, tearing apart communities via eminent domain, and enabling disinvestment within their neighborhoods. To promote equality of opportunity and outcome within the housing space, we must acknowledge our past faults and actively dismantle such discriminatory structures. With that being said, as Chair of the Housing Committee, I am proud to announce the 2023 Council Housing Strategy–a comprehensive legislative package that will promote the construction of new affordable housing units, establish new protections for tenants, and increase opportunities for lower-income families to achieve homeownership More information about the proposed legislation can be found later in this newsletter.

 

In the rest of this newsletter, you will read more about happenings in the City Council and in my Office. As always, I represent you and would love to hear your thoughts! Please feel free to reach out to my office at 614-645-5524.

2023 Council Housing Strategy

As Chair of the Housing Committee, I am proud of the work we have done to ensure more equitable access to stable, safe, and affordable housing. In 2021, we passed the Housing for All legislative package, which provided basic protections to renters, including flexibility with security deposit payments and preventing landlords from discriminating against tenant applicants based on the source of income. This year, we are building upon that foundation through our 2023 Council Housing Strategy. Our goal is threefold: we want to reinvest in our city through the sustainable development of new affordable housing units, preserve our current housing stocks, and ensure the housing market is inclusive of all peoples, regardless of socio-economic status.

 

We value public input and hope that this legislation sparks a new conversation within Columbus as to how we can address our looming crisis in a beneficial manner for the many communities that call this city home. As such, these policies are not set-in-stone; they are a starting point in a dialogue between council and the public. We are excited to engage with all of our constituents to solicit feedback and build upon these proposals. Each Councilmember will be leading a policy initiative in collaboration with the rest of the City Council Team. This is a collaborative effort, not just amongst those at City Hall, but with the entire Columbus Community. With that being said, here is an outline of the housing strategy:

 

Investment:

  • Homeownership Opportunities: Providing financial support to enable all residents to have the opportunity to own a home.
  • ADUnit Pilot Program: Through promoting the use of accessory dwelling units (ADUs), the City will be able to increase the housing supply to better meet demand and drive down housing costs.

Preservation:

  • Vacant and Foreclosure Registry: Would create more accountability measures for property owners and managers through requiring them to register the properties they own. Further, fees would be levied against those who own vacant properties, which often prompt disinvestment and crime. 
  • Senior Home Repair Program: Would provide funding for senior citizens to make necessary home repairs that enable them to remain in their homes and maintain their accumulated generational wealth.
  • Wholesaler Regulation Legislation: Real estate wholesalers are businesses that seek to purchase large numbers of homes and properties for very little and then sell them to developers for profit. Predictably, it is a practice that often exploits lower-income families who are in desperate need of quick cash. This proposal would stop such predatory practices through creating licensed regulations similar to that of a realtor.

Inclusion:

  • Pay to Stay - This proposal would allow residents additional time to secure rental assistance without fear of losing their homes or having an eviction judgment on their records.
  • Citywide Community Reinvestment Area: This program would instate tax incentives for investing into real property improvements and new housing developments, making housing more affordable citywide.
  • Retaliatory Action: This will strengthen and clarify language from legislation passed in 2018 to protect renters from retaliatory action.
  • Third Party Payment: Would require property owners and managers to accept rent payments from a third party payment source.
  • Rent Increase Notification: Would require landlords to provide notice of a rent increase 180 days before it occurs.
  • Office of Fair Housing: Create an office of fair housing to serve as the city’s hub for anything relating to equitable housing practices. The office’s guiding goal would be to protect the rights and needs of tenants, holding landlords and property owners accountable when they do not fulfill their responsibilities.
  • Legal Representation at Eviction Court: Legal representation is a right within the U.S. and it's imperative that those facing eviction have access to it. In 2022, Council legislated $1.5M to create a more robust legal representation team at eviction court and this proposal will fund an additional year of work.
  • Columbus Rental Registry: This proposal would collect a rental registration fee, generating millions of dollars to be used for rental assistance, and encourage both owners and occupants to maintain and improve the quality of rental housing.

Columbus plans to beef up rental laws, improve affordable housing (dispatch.com)

 

What housing policies will Columbus City Council consider in 2023? (nbc4i.com)

Council Spotlight

On March 13th, City Council passed an ordinance that would effectively ban Columbus employers from inquiring into an applicant’s credit or salary history. The goal of this legislation is to increase pay equity within the city, especially for women and BIPOC. Oftentimes, salary information requirements disadvantage these communities as they rely upon a false equivalency of a worker’s value and their respective salary. I am proud to have voted for this legislation and look forward to continuing advancing the cause of fair pay within Columbus.

 

On March 20th, City Council passed legislation that amended rules governing the operation and licensing of Mobile Food Vendors. The goals of this legislation were to update parts of the previous code that were outdated. The major changes include:

  • Creating an online reservation system that enables vendors to create temporary permits.
  • Reconstitutes the Mobile Food Vending Board.
  • Clarifying law enforcements’ authority to enforce sections of the code.
  • Requires mobile food vendors to cease operations by 2:30 am and to be out of the right-of-way by 3:00am in the Short North Area.

Health & Human Services

These monies will help the agency fund grants that provide vital health services to members of our communities, including family planning services and HIV screening and protection programs. 

Housing

  • To celebrate National Fair Housing Month, we are introducing a resolution at Council’s April 3rd meeting to proclaim April as “Fair Housing Month” in Columbus. The city’s fair housing partner, the Legal Aid of Society of Columbus, will accept and present the resolution.

Criminal Justice & Judiciary

March 2023 • Columbus City Council

Happy Women’s History Month!

March marks the beginning of Women’s History Month, a period for us to reflect upon the historical, cultural, political, and economic contributions of women across the United States. It is also a time for us to recommit to the cause of gender equality; throughout American history, women have often faced political marginalization, having their rights neglected or even forcibly taken away. Unfortunately, this isn’t something of the past as we all witnessed the overturning of Roe v. Wade in June 2022. 

 

This year’s theme is “Celebrating Women Who Tell our Stories,” an ode to the legendary women who have paved the path for us all to walk on and to each of our unique lived experiences. Women like Shirley Chisholm, the first Black women to be elected to Congress, Patsy Mink, the champion of the Title IX protections in the Higher Education Act, and Gloria Stenim, a leader of the women’s right movement in the 60’s, fought not just for equal rights for women, but championed the principle of equality for all. Being a woman is not a monolithic experience, it is one shaped by the intersectionality of our identities. Yet, it is the sum of these stories, the hardships we have faced, and our journey to overcoming them that define us as a community-one that uplifts each other and fights for our collective right to live freely.

 

To this day, women still face a litany of obstacles. As of 2020, on average, women earn $0.82 to the man’s $1.00. Gender norms still restrict the career mobility of women who seek to start a family. The “pink tax”-the extra amount of money women are charged for products specifically marketed towards them-costs women an estimated $1,300 a year. Further, women remain disproportionately under-represented in places of power: as of 2023, women occupied 53 CEO slots in Fortune 500 companies and just 147 of 535 seats within the 118th Congress.

 

Representation matters. These inequities will not be resolved until the voices of women, and specifically women of color, are actively heard and listened to. On Council, we are proud of the work we have done to improve gender equality within Columbus, passing laws to protect women experiencing domestic violence, providing free women’s hygiene products at all city recreation centers, among others.

 

In the rest of this newsletter, you will read more about happenings in the City Council

and in my Office. As always, I represent you and would love to hear your thoughts! Please do not hesitate to call my office at 614-965-8297.

Woman-owned Business Highlight

Zora's House

Named for Zora Neale Hurston, a woman of extraordinary brilliance and fiery spirit, Zora’s House is a sanctuary for women and gender-expansive people of color to dream, connect, and create; to shine bright and inspire change.  Where you don’t have to worry about what your hair looks like or how loud you get.  Where you can shine in the center of attention or find quiet solitude.  Where you have your lightbulb moment or take your ideas back to the drawing board.  It’s a world dedicated to the legacies of our foremothers — our mama, our aunties, our grandmothers — the people who found ways to connect and succeed and grow in a world not created with them in mind.  Zora’s House is a workplace.   A haven.   A happy hour.   An incubator.  A community for women and non-binary people of color committed to transforming themselves and the world around them.

 

Words from the founder: “I’ve always believed that a world in which women, especially women of color, are taught to dream big, completely disregard the status quo, and create lives and careers they love, is a better world for everybody. Zora’s House is an organization dedicated to helping myself – and other women like me – do just that.”

 

Council Happenings

On February 6th, City Council voted to initiate an administrative process that could shift the speed limit of the downtown streets from 35 mph to 25 mph. It is imperative we ensure the safety of pedestrians and cyclists, and this change will do that. Studies have demonstrated that the survival rate of a pedestrian hit by a vehicle increases from 10% to 90% by dropping the speed from 40 mph to 20 mph. Before this policy is officially implemented, a study must be conducted by the State Department of Transportation.

 

Councilmember Rob Dorans was elected as the city’s President Pro Tempore of Council upon the departure of former Councilmember Elizabeth Brown. President Pro Tem Dorans has served on Council since 2020 and is the chair of the Building and Zoning, Workforce Development, Zoning, and Public Utilities Committees. I look forward to continuing to work with him for actions and policies that benefit the entire Columbus Community!

Committee Highlights

Health & Human Services

  • This month we’re also celebrating Kidney Disease Awareness Month, with a resolution slated to be voted on at the March 6th meeting. Join us in spreading awareness and fighting for more equitable access to preventative screenings!
    • Nearly 1 in 10 individuals experience Kidney Disease, including nearly 10 million Ohioans. Health impacts can include higher risk for heart disease, anemia, and even kidney failure.
  • Voted to extend a contract with the YMCA of Central Ohio to continue providing rental and utility assistance to low-income residents of Columbus.
    • At least 60% of the funding will support households making at or less than 60% of the area median income (AMI), up to 40% can be used for households at 80% or below, and up to 15% of the funding can be used for administrative costs.

Housing

  • On February 6th, Council voted to amend a previous piece of legislation passed that would ensure the creation of a new affordable housing development-The Columbus Renaissance Housing development- in a timely and cost-effective manner.
    • This project is located at 33 West Morrill Avenue in Merion village and will feature nearly 45 units, all being at or below 60% of the AMI.

Community Development for All People (CD4AP), with the support of funding from Columbus City Council, has launched a non-profit social enterprise called the South End Café. The Café is designed to provide good-paying jobs to those who are having a hard time finding employment, such as returning citizens and those who have been out of the workforce for an extended period of time. Positions in the Café are given to people without prior experience, and employees will gain a work history and practical training in skills that they will leverage into full-time, career track employment opportunities.

 

In addition to great coffee, the Café will provide a place for community members to gather for meetings, activities, and socialization. Soon, the Café will also offer affordable, healthy meals in a neighborhood where access to healthy food is limited and is anticipated to spur additional redevelopment in the area.

February 7, 2023 • Columbus City Council

Happy Black History Month

February marks the start of Black History Month, a time of celebration and reflection on the historical contributions of Black Americans. More importantly, it also serves as a time to consider the systemic injustices still harming Black and Brown peoples across this city, state, and nation, and recommit ourselves to pursuing true equality under the law.

 

This year’s theme is “Black Resistance,” a nod toward the daily struggle of Black Americans, both today and historically, against a constant stream of oppression. Against the brutality of lynching, Jim Crow, and police violence-to name just a few-, Black Americans have remained steadfast in their efforts to build a truly just democracy. Icons like Martin Luther King Jr., Harriet Tubman, John Lewis, among countless more, devoted their lives to the cause and are examples of whom we all should strive to be-regardless of race. Further, this theme has an added salience in regard to the senseless murder of Tyre Nichols. Our governing institutions, like the police, were built to oppress black and brown people. Systemic and institutionalized racism are alive and well and we must do everything in our power to act, advocating for and passing common sense reforms to prevent a tragedy like this from ever happening again. My heart goes out to Tyre’s family and the Memphis community while they heal from this loss.

 

While there is still so much work that needs to be done to ensure racial justice in Columbus, we have taken concrete steps toward reducing and eliminating disparities. One recent effort includes a partnership between City Council, the city development department, the Columbus Coalition for the Homeless, and Community Development for All People to open community warming shelters through the Winter. In 2021, it was reported that Black Americans comprise nearly 39% of the population of people experiencing homelessness. Creating warming shelters is a much needed short-term fix, but we must fight to create more affordable housing within the City so that all people can have a safe place to live.

 

In the rest of this newsletter, you will read more about happenings in the City Council and in my Office. As always, I represent you and would love to hear your thoughts! Please do not hesitate to call my office at 614-965-8297.

Black Business Highlight

GRND - 1106-1108 E Main St. Columbus, Ohio 43205

We are a membership-based co-working and social lounge creating the space to both ground and grind. Taking the “I” out of the “grind”, we connect and cultivate an engaged community of real people building our collective power, while practicing self-care along the way. We work hard - but we also take time to celebrate wins. 

 

GRND’s founders Sean and Jennifer Walton, and William and Layla Lumpkin have spent the last two decades of friendship building community with one another and GRND is their opportunity to extend that gift outward. What started out as a dream of a space where values-aligned folks could come and build together, quickly manifested into that vision and more: a love letter to Black Columbus that honors our past, embraces our present, and makes room for the future. GRND is a space where members can feel grounded, honored, safe, and empowered to grind collectively. If we wanted to go fast, we’d go alone, but we want to go far, so we go together.

Council Spotlight

  • On January 9th, City Council voted to make Mitchell Brown former Council Member Elizabeth Brown’s successor. This marks a second stint on council for Council Member Designate Mitchell Brown as he previously served from 2016-2021. I look forward to working with him to continue bettering the City we both love!
  • In December, City Council passed gun safety legislation that would ban possession of large-capacity magazines of 30+ rounds and create penalties for those who do not properly store firearms from the reach of children or sell a gun to someone prohibited from owning one. The Ohio Attorney General’s Office sued the city charging that the legislation was unconstitutional, however, a recent court ruling is allowing implementation starting January 21st. This legislation will help ensure residents of Columbus remain safe from the growing epidemic of gun violence across the country.

Committee Spotlights

Health & Human Services

  • This month we’re also celebrating National Wear Red Day on February 3rd. This day is meant to bring awareness to heart disease, a leading cause of death within the U.S. The CDC estimates that nearly 1 person dies every 34 seconds from cardiovascular disease. I will be wearing red to help raise and spread awareness of efforts to eradicate heart disease; I hope you join me!

Housing

  • City Council approved $200,000 to conduct a marketing and engagement campaign around the Housing for All legislative package I introduced in 2021.
  • At its February 6th meeting, Council approved $125,000 to support the Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) Pilot Project, one of our efforts to make housing more affordable within the Columbus real estate market.
    • ADU’s are smaller buildings and/or homes located on the same lot as a larger house, thereby increasing the overall housing supply and reducing housing prices.

2023 Operating Budget Highlight

2023 Operating Budget Highlights 

On February 6th, Columbus City Council hosted a press conference to share amendments to the 2023 Operating Budget. City budgets are a reflection of our collective values; they provide us with a blueprint for how the city will operate and the policies it will pursue in the coming year. It is absolutely vital that the 2023 Operating Budget is reflective of the ENTIRE Columbus community, and as such, we have hosted tens of hearings across the city to solicit grassroots feedback and spending requests.

 

This budget has three major themes: safety, workforce development, and housing. We occupy a unique place in Columbus history: our city is experiencing sky-rocketing growth and we must act to ensure that everyone, regardless of background, can have a fair shot at taking part in these exciting opportunities. To do so, we must ensure our city is equipped with resources to protect its citizens, that Columbus residents have access to good-paying jobs to support their families, and that affordable housing is not just a talking point but a reality. 

Here are just a few policies this budget will help advance:

  • $1.5 Million in funding to ensure individuals and families facing eviction have access to quality legal representation.
  • Funding for the Senior Home Repair Program, a policy which provides financial assistance to older residents of Columbus for home maintenance projects that have a positive impact on their health and safety.

  • $200,000 to continue the Housing for All community education campaign to promote rental protections and rights of residents.

November 24, 2022 • Columbus City Council

Happy Thanksgiving from Shayla Favor!

Thanksgiving is a time to join with family and friends and give thanks for the blessings that we enjoy every day. I am thankful for my loving family, and supportive colleagues, and so appreciative of the opportunity to serve these last 4 years as a Columbus City Councilmember. 

However above all, I know our City’s true resilience, kindness and diversity comes from you, our residents. So thank YOU for your engagement and interest in making your community a wonderful place to live. I’m also thankful for all of our City staff, who work tirelessly each and every day to ensure the safety of our roads, schools, and neighborhoods. 

There is a lot to be grateful for, but I’d be remiss if I did not mention my gratitude for everything our Hunger Heroes have done and continue to do to address hunger in our community, not only this thanksgiving season but year-round.

This fall, I toured Mid-Ohio Food Collective’s distribution center to learn more about their important efforts to serve families across Central Ohio. From giving fresh produce to families to collaborating with community partners to expand the reach of services- there’s no doubt food banks play a vital role in our community. According to the  Local Food Action Plan for the City of Columbus and Franklin County study, nearly 60% of Black households are food insecure in comparison to white households. I am truly thankful for the Mid-Ohio Food Collective, its community partners, and over 4,000 volunteers who work tirelessly to help end hunger and bring hope to some of our most food-insecure households. As we continue to approach the holiday season please monitor my social media to learn more about how you can help your fellow Columbus residents in need. 

It’s important to me that we remove the stigma around who hunger affects. This is why I look forward to continuing my support for Mid-Ohio Food Collective and community partners addressing food insecurity in Columbus.

Please sign up here to receive a Holiday card from me!

What’s Happening in My Office

Council Spotlight

On October 22nd, the Columbus City Council Women’s Caucus celebrated its inaugural Columbus Girls Summit: Igniting your Political Power. We were pleased to host dozens of young women in chambers! The state of women’s leadership in government has always remained an important topic, but the need to increase women’s leadership and political participation has increased for many reasons, including the recent overturning of Roe v. Wade. There is no doubt women are underrepresented in politics, and as a result, policies impacting reproductive rights are oftentimes rolled out without the support of the communities they impact. This is why it is important to me and my colleagues, Councilmembers Elizabeth Brown and Councilmember Lourdes Barroso de Padilla, that we invest in leadership programming focused on empowering and equipping our young women and girls with the tools necessary to lead. 

 At our inaugural Columbus Girls Summit, the Columbus Women’s Caucus aimed to create a space for women-identifying young individuals to have their voices heard in the political process. It was an amazing experience and we look forward to continuing this event every year. By empowering the women that will come after us we arm the next generation with hope.

 

Please follow my social media for the latest updates on the Columbus Women’s Caucus.

Housing Corner

This month I had the opportunity to authorize an important piece of legislation aimed at understanding the impacts of eviction on low-income tenants and the City as well as the benefits that could be realized if low-income tenants were represented in eviction proceedings. 

  • Allocated $100,000.00 for the Director of the Department of Development to enter into a contract with Stout Risius Ross, LLC.

An eviction causes housing instability and has long-lasting effects on other facets of an individual's life. Eviction Lab, which collects data from Franklin County Municipal Courts, found that just last week that nearly 430 cases were filed and that since March 2020 that over 40,000 cases were filed. With this $100,000 contract, Stout Risius Ross, LLC. will be able to work with both the Franklin County Board of Commissioners and the City of Columbus to gather data on the impacts of eviction on low-income tenants and the City as well as the benefits that could be realized if low-income tenants were represented in eviction proceedings. 

Health and Human Services

During the month of October, Columbus City Council authorized the Board of Health to accept grant funds from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in an effort to improve access to medical care for individuals living with HIV or AIDS. 

  • Direct the Board of Health to accept grant funds in the amount of $3,334,529.00 and any additional funds for the Ryan White Part A HIV Care grant program.

The Ryan White Part A (RWPA) HIV Care grant aims to improve access to medical care for individuals living with HIV or AIDS living in Central Ohio. The goal is that each individual will achieve viral suppression, which improves their quality of life and reduces the risk of spreading the infection.  This grant will enhance medical services for both somatic and behavioral health, pay for HIV-related doctor’s visits, mental health services, substance abuse services, and other services allowable by the grant, and strengthen the case management and linkage to care programs at CPH.

On October 29th, The Ohio Women Against Domestic Violence hosted its inaugural survivor walk. The Ohio Women Against Domestic Violence works to raise awareness of Domestic Violence by educating communities on the necessity of developing and maintaining healthy relationships and offering supportive resources through their community-based networks. Domestic violence impacts men, women, and children of every age, background, and belief. Nearly 1 in 3 women and 1 in 4 men in the United States have suffered abuse from an intimate partner, and in 2020 there were more than 15, 259 domestic violence calls in Columbus and Central Ohio.

October 12, 2022 • Columbus Councilmember Shayla Favor 

Igniting Change Within Our Community 

As we approach the beginning of Fall, the season of change, we must recommit ourselves to igniting the change we want to see in our community. Last month, the Lewis family mourned the terrible death of 20 year-old Donovan Lewis, who was killed by a Columbus Police Officer. Our Community is reeling from yet another loss of a young black man. As the investigation into the fatal shooting continues,  my colleagues and I at Columbus City Council remain committed to reimagining public safety and as chair of the Criminal Justice and Judiciary Committee, I will continue to advocate for the  review of City policies that disproportionately impact Black and Brown communities. All aspects of our daily life continue to be affected by racism in some way. From Black residents walking down the street to corporate boardrooms,  Black individuals confront this reality everyday. On September 21st, I joined the Columbus Women’s Commission’s Black Women’s Equal Pay Day campaign. Today, Black women earn fifty-eight cents to every dollar earned by white men and eighty-three cents to that of white women. Too often commemorative days like Black Women's Equal Pay Day come and go without any real opportunity for reflection. But one thing is for certain-- Black women deserve to be paid fairly for their work and we must ensure that they are. Here are some steps that employers can take to ensure that their workers are getting paid their worth: 

  • Employers can begin to conduct routine compensation audits that examine the racial, ethnic, and gender pay difference, provide greater job transparency, and provide anti-bias training to all employees with a special emphasis to hiring managers. 
  • Tools Women can utilize to feel empowered when addressing the pay gap in the workplace. 
  • It's Equal Pay Day—Here Are 4 Things You Can Do Today to Close the Gap.

By taking these action steps, Black women will begin to get paid what they deserve.

Council Spotlight

During the week of  September 19, City Hall was illuminated red in honor of sickle Cell Awareness Month. As Health Chair, it is important to me that we support organizations uplifting  families battling Sickle Cell disease and work together to spotlight the disproportionate impact Sickle Cell disease has on African-Americans. It is reported  that 1 out of every 500   African-American children are born with sickle cell anemia. Sickle Cell Disease is most common in people from the continent of Africa or African-Americans, but can also be found in other ethnic and racial groups, including people from South and Central America, the Caribbean, the Mediterranean, and India.   As a long-time advocate, it was an honor to present the Health Champion Award to former Councilmember Priscilla Tyson. Tyson dedicated her life to bringing awareness to Sickle Cell Disease and the importance of early testing. 

Many important observances occur in September, but one of most memorable moments for me was honoring Childhood Cancer Awareness Month. On September 19th, I declared September as Childhood Cancer Awareness Month in the City of Columbus. Each year, 16,790 children are diagnosed with cancer in the United States. Additionally, half of childhood cancer families will be faced with significant out-of-pocket expenses. Remaining committed to raising awareness about the effects of childhood cancer on children, but also on their families, must remain on the forefront of our community’s minds.

Committee Updates:

Housing Corner

This past month, I had the opportunity to pass two important pieces of legislation:

 

  • Providing $9.5 million in emergency rental assistance to IMPACT Community Action
  • Providing funds to the Community Shelter Board to establish a transitional Housing Pilot Program. 

According to a report published by Rentometer, Columbus renters have seen an increase of  twenty-seven percent in the past year--- meaning that Columbus saw the largest increase in the midwest region. With authorizing an additional $9.5 million dollars in emergency rental assistance, the City of Columbus is providing Columbus renters with the financial help that they need to remain in their homes and focus on their families and other aspects of their lives. There is a lot more work needed to address the underlying Central Ohio housing crisis, so in the coming months I look forward to introducing Housing for All 2.0 to address these very concerns. 

Lastly, with the establishment of this transitional Housing Pilot Program we are allowing formerly unhoused individuals, who were staying at an outdoor encampment, to now reside in a safe and stable environment as they go through the process of securing long-term housing. Program participants are receiving bus passes, hotel lodging, meals, and individualized case management as they work to transition into permanent housing. In doing so, we hope to further provide unhoused residents with the assistance that they need to get the safe housing that they deserve.

Health and Human Services:

During the month of September, I legislated two pieces of legislation aimed at providing funds for HIV prevention and surveillance programs. 

 

  • Authorized Columbus Board of Health to accept $1.2 million dollars in funds for HIV Prevention programs. 
  • Authorized the Board of Health to enter contracts with vendors for the Implementing Enhanced HIV Prevention and Surveillance of Health Departments to End the HIV Epidemic in Ohio Grant Program.

With the establishment of these programs, pillars of diagnosis and prevention remain the two drivers of the city council’s efforts in providing treatment to Columbus residents. In 2020, there were 897 reported new diagnoses of HIV within the state of Ohio, with fifty-two percent of new diagnoses were among Black/African American people. The rate of new diagnoses among Black/African American people was nearly eight times higher  in comparison to white people.The earlier that someone is diagnosed as living with HIV, the earlier life-saving treatment can start. Like many other diseases, the earlier that HIV treatment starts after infection, the better the outcome. Columbus residents who are diagnosed with HIV can live long and healthy lives with early detection of HIV and proper treatment and care.

Community Spotlight

On September 17th, Education Foundation for Freedom hosted its annual Columbus Women and Girls’ Fest. During the  festival, I highlighted the efforts of The Education Foundation for Freedom and my support for funding for programs including the Women & Girls’ festival.  in hosting immersive educational experiences that stress the importance of the arts, literacy, entrepreneurship, community responsibility, and wellness. The Foundation helps to mobilize women and girl-identified people of color in often overlooked areas of Columbus and becomes a launching platform for them to achieve success.

item.title: Shayla Favor's Yearly Recap
item.description:
September 7, 2022 • Columbus Councilmember Shayla Favor 

Reflections and Plans for 2022

As we approach the end of summer, this time provides us with a moment to reflect on the tremendous work we have been able to achieve in our city’s legislative process, our communities, and our city, while also readying ourselves for continuing to make change. I am proud to share that in just the first 8 months of 2022, I have: 

  • Launched the ‘Pathways to Purpose: Casey Goodson Jr. CDL Program’ in honor of Casey Goodson Jr., which provides resources and the skills for people to become CDL trained drivers
  • Allocated additional funding to support Columbus Legal Aid’s services at the Franklin County Eviction Court.

In response to the overturn of Roe V. Wade, the City Council’s Women’s Caucus passed a comprehensive legislative package to protect reproductive rights, which includes: 

  • The creation of a $1M abortion access fund for fund to Planned Parenthood of Greater Ohio, Ohio's Women Alliance and Abortion Fund of Ohio.
  • Legislation that aims to de-prioritize the criminalization of pregnancy outcomes.
  • The implementation of a secret shopper survey that aims to protect residents from false or misleading information by examining activities at crisis pregnancy centers. 

Despite the tremendous work we have done to level the playing field and protect renters in the city of Columbus by passing legislation that prohibits Source of Income discrimination, requires rental payment receipts, and security deposit payment options for tenants-- we still have more work to do. In the coming weeks, my office will begin rolling out the Housing for All 2.0 legislative package, which will provide additional protections for renters.  Additionally, we will continue to work on legislation to support the reproductive rights of residents, address our city’s Black maternal health crisis, and roll out a comprehensive Equity Action Plan.

Stay up to date with the latest my office is doing by subscribing to my monthly newsletter or follow me on my Instagram, Twitter and Facebook pages!

 

What’s Happening in My Office

Equity in Action 

  • Racial Equity Collaborative: In 2020, Columbus City Council created the Racial Equity Collaborative, an internal equity team focused on supporting the community’s access to opportunity while empowering all residents to engage with local government. Further, in the month of August, the collaborative began to focus its efforts on reviewing internal policies and practices to ensure that the City is being equitable and inclusive. More updates are to come but I look forward to continuing the promises and efforts made in light of the city-wide protests in response to the death of George Floyd.
  • Columbus Youth Council: When I joined Council in 2019, I created the Columbus Youth Council to provide High School students, from various racial and socio-economic backgrounds, the opportunity to learn about city government and how they can become the stewards of tomorrow. We are now going into our third year, and I could not be happier to continue in this tradition of equipping our students with the knowledge of the inner workings of city government, economic development, and capping the program with a trip to Washington, D.C. to lobby state and federal leaders. If you are, or know any, high school students encourage them to apply at the following website: https://www.columbus.gov/council/News-and-Media/Councilmember-Shayla-Favor-Announces-Youth-Council-for-Columbus-City-Schools-Students/.

Council Spotlight

Abortion Access Legislative Package

This summer millions of women, and birth-giving individuals, were stripped of their fundamental rights and access to healthcare. In particular, the overturning of these rights will inflict irreversible harm on minorities, particularly Black and low-income individuals who rely heavily on the right to an abortion. 

 

As chair of the Health and Human Services committee, I felt it was critical to respond quickly to our state’s restrictive abortion laws. In response to the Dobbs decision by the Supreme Court, Columbus City Council's women's caucus championed three pieces of legislation to protect reproductive access. By creating a million-dollar fund for Planned Parenthood of Greater Ohio, Ohio's Women Alliance, and Abortion Fund of Ohio. The second piece of legislation allows the city to enter into a contract with Pro-Choice Ohio to conduct a secret shopper survey which aims to report pregnancy centers providing misleading and inaccurate information to residents.  As the legislative session resumes I look forward to working with my colleagues, stakeholders, and community members to champion more legislation. Read more about our efforts at council in the  Columbus Dispatch.  

Committee Updates:

Housing Corner

This past June, I had the pleasure of hosting our first Housing for All Event! In 2021, I championed three pieces of legislation which were geared toward removing barriers and protecting Columbus tenants . The 2021 legislative package prohibited source of income discrimination, requires landlords to provide receipts when rental payments are received, allows residents to choose security deposit payment plans. At the town hall, residents had the opportunity to hear from a panel of stakeholders and gather resources from housing social service providers to add to their toolkits. While this legislation moved us in the right direction, I know more needs to be done and acknowledge the reality that many residents continue to encounter housing challenges. In the coming months, my office will begin rolling out additional legislation to further protect and reduce barriers for Columbus residents. The event can be watched here.

Remembering Casey Goodson Jr.

Last year, I championed the Pathways to Purpose: Casey Goodson Jr. CDL Program which provides an opportunity for Columbus residents to obtain their Commercial Driver's License. Before Casey Goodson Jr. was tragically shot he was an experienced CDL driver, who loved his community and family. So, it was important for me that we honor his legacy and family-driven spirit by creating a CDL program to ensure that there are quality opportunities for individuals regardless of their backgrounds. By partnering with IMPACT Community Action and The Capital Transportation Academy's Roads2Work program, we are not only working to address the shortage of CDL drivers in the Central Ohio region but are also equipping Columbus residents with the experience needed to obtain a middle class job.

Community Spotlight

On August 18th, The Central Ohio Restored Citizens Collaborative hosted its 10th annual Restored Citizen Summit at Columbus State Community College. The coalition’s mission is to challenge the narrative that often surrounds people affected by the criminal justice system and connects them to social service providers and community stakeholders to ease their transition. In April, I sponsored resolution 0069X-2022 which recognized National Reentry week in Columbus! To learn more about The Central Ohio Restored Citizens Collaborative, visit https://www.centralohiorcc.com/ .
